3-1: Welcome to Fang Math. This is Geometry, lesson 3 point 1: Pairs of Lines & Angles.
Two lines in space can relate in three ways. First, they can be intersecting: they meet at exactly one point.
Second, they can be parallel. Parallel lines lie in the same plane and never meet.
Third, they can be skew. Skew lines never meet, but they are not in the same plane. Skew lines only happen in three dimensions.
Let's use a box. Line A B and line D C are both on the top face, and they never meet. So they are parallel.
Line A B and line B F share point B. So they are intersecting.
Line A B and line C G never meet, and no flat face contains both of them. So they are skew.
Planes can be parallel too. The top face and the bottom face never meet, so they are parallel planes.
A transversal is a line that crosses two other lines. Here, line t crosses lines l and m, and it makes eight angles.
Angles one to four are at the top crossing. Angles five to eight are at the bottom crossing, in the same positions.
Angles between the two lines are called interior. Angles outside the two lines are called exterior.
Now let's name the pairs. Corresponding angles are in the same position at each crossing, like angle one and angle five.
Alternate interior angles are inside the two lines, on opposite sides of the transversal, like angle four and angle five.
Alternate exterior angles are outside the two lines, on opposite sides, like angle one and angle eight.
And same side interior angles are inside, on the same side of the transversal, like angle three and angle five.
Watch out. Two lines that never meet are not always parallel. If you can't find one flat plane that contains both, they are skew.
Your turn. Name each pair. Angle two and angle six. Angle three and angle six. Angle four and angle six. Pause the video and try it.|

Angles two and six are in the same position, so they are corresponding. Angles three and six are inside, on opposite sides, so they are alternate interior. Angles four and six are inside, on the same side, so they are same side interior.

Remember: two lines can be intersecting, parallel or skew. A transversal makes eight angles, and we name the pairs corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior, and same side interior. Now go to fang math dot com and practice at your level. See you next time!
3-2: Welcome to Fang Math. This is Geometry, lesson 3 point 2: Parallel Lines & Transversals.
When the two lines are parallel, the angle pairs have special relationships. Corresponding angles are congruent.
Alternate interior angles are congruent, and alternate exterior angles are congruent too.
But same side interior angles are supplementary. They add up to one hundred eighty degrees.
Here's the easy way to remember it. When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, there are only two sizes of angle: a small acute one and a big obtuse one.
Any two acute angles are equal. Any two obtuse angles are equal.
And an acute angle plus an obtuse angle always makes one hundred eighty degrees.
Let's try one. Lines l and m are parallel, and angle one is one hundred ten degrees. Find angle five and angle six.
Angles one and five are corresponding, so they are congruent. Angle five is one hundred ten degrees.
Angles five and six form a linear pair, so angle six is one eighty minus one ten, which is seventy degrees.
Now with algebra. Two alternate interior angles are three x plus fifteen and five x minus twenty five.
Since the lines are parallel, alternate interior angles are congruent. Set them equal. Three x plus fifteen equals five x minus twenty five. So forty equals two x, and x is twenty.
Then the angle is three times twenty plus fifteen, which is seventy five degrees. Always answer the question they asked.
Watch out. Same side interior angles are not equal. They add to one hundred eighty. So set up the equation with a sum of one eighty.
Your turn. The lines are parallel. Same side interior angles are two x plus ten, and three x minus five. Find x and both angles. Pause the video and try it.|
They add to one eighty. Five x plus five equals one eighty, so x is thirty five. The angles are eighty degrees and one hundred degrees. Check: eighty plus one hundred is one eighty.

Remember: when lines are parallel, corresponding and alternate angles are congruent, and same side interior angles add to one eighty. Acute equals acute, obtuse equals obtuse, and acute plus obtuse is one eighty. Now go to fang math dot com and practice at your level. See you next time!
3-3: Welcome to Fang Math. This is Geometry, lesson 3 point 3: Proving Lines Parallel.
In the last lesson we started with parallel lines and found angles. Now we go backwards.
If the angles are right, then the lines must be parallel. These are called converses.
If corresponding angles are congruent, the lines are parallel.
If alternate interior angles are congruent, or alternate exterior angles are congruent, the lines are parallel.
If same side interior angles are supplementary, the lines are parallel.
And one more: if two lines are both parallel to a third line, they are parallel to each other.
Angle four is seventy two degrees, and angle five is seventy two degrees. Are lines l and m parallel? Don't assume it. Prove it.
First, name the pair. Angles four and five are alternate interior angles.
They have the same measure, so they are congruent. By the alternate interior angles converse, l is parallel to m.
Same side interior angles are four x plus six, and five x minus fifteen. For what x are the lines parallel?
For same side interior angles, we need them to add to one eighty. Nine x minus nine equals one eighty, so nine x is one eighty nine, and x is twenty one.
Watch out. Never say the lines look parallel. Name the angle pair, show it is congruent or supplementary, and then name the converse you used.
Your turn. Angle one is one hundred fifteen degrees, and angle eight is one hundred fifteen degrees. Are the lines parallel? Which converse proves it? Pause the video and try it.|
Angles one and eight are alternate exterior angles, and they are congruent. So yes, the lines are parallel, by the alternate exterior angles converse.

Remember: if corresponding or alternate angles are congruent, the lines are parallel. If same side interior angles are supplementary, the lines are parallel. Name the pair, show the angle fact, and name the converse. Now go to fang math dot com and practice at your level. See you next time!
3-4: Welcome to Fang Math. This is Geometry, lesson 3 point 4: Perpendicular Lines.
Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, ninety degrees. We write a, upside down T, b.
In a picture, a little square at the corner marks the right angle.
Angles one and two form a linear pair, so they add to one eighty.
If they are also congruent, each one is one eighty divided by two, which is ninety degrees.
So: if two lines form a linear pair of congruent angles, the lines are perpendicular.
In a plane, if two lines are both perpendicular to the same line, then they are parallel to each other.
Why? Both lines make ninety degree corresponding angles with the transversal. Congruent corresponding angles mean the lines are parallel.
How far is point P from line l? Drop a segment from P straight down to the line, so it is perpendicular. Call the foot Q.
Any slanted path from P to the line is longer. The red dashed paths are longer than P Q.
So the distance from a point to a line is the length of the perpendicular segment. It's the shortest path.
Watch out. Only the perpendicular segment gives the distance to a line. A slanted segment is always too long.
Your turn. Point P is at three, five, and the line is y equals one. What is the distance from P to the line? Pause the video and try it.|
The line is horizontal, so go straight down to three, one. The distance is five minus one, which is four.

Remember: perpendicular lines meet at ninety degrees. A linear pair of congruent angles means the lines are perpendicular. And the distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular segment, the shortest path. Now go to fang math dot com and practice at your level. See you next time!
3-5: Welcome to Fang Math. This is Geometry, lesson 3 point 5: Equations of Parallel & Perpendicular Lines.
On a coordinate grid, parallel lines have the same slope. They rise at exactly the same rate.
Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals.
That means flip the fraction, and change the sign. Two thirds becomes negative three halves. And their product is negative one.
Start with y equals two thirds x plus one. The slope is two thirds.
A parallel line has the same slope, two thirds.
A perpendicular line has the slope negative three halves.
Write the line through two, three that is parallel to y equals four x minus one.
Parallel, so the slope is four. Use point slope form: y minus three equals four times x minus two.
Distribute and add three: y equals four x minus five.
Now a perpendicular line through four, one, perpendicular to two x plus three y equals six.
First solve for y to find the slope. Y equals negative two thirds x plus two. The slope is negative two thirds.
Flip and change the sign: three halves. So y minus one equals three halves times x minus four. That gives y equals three halves x minus five.
Watch out. Perpendicular needs both steps, flip and change the sign. The perpendicular slope of two is negative one half, not one half.
Your turn. Write the line through three, negative two that is perpendicular to y equals negative three x plus seven. Pause the video and try it.|
The slope negative three flips to one third. Y plus two equals one third times x minus three. So y equals one third x minus three.

Remember: parallel lines have the same slope. Perpendicular lines have negative reciprocal slopes: flip and change the sign. Then use point slope form. Now go to fang math dot com and practice at your level. See you next time!
